extracted.intended_audience: poets, orators, students of rhetoric, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing 'the Sublime' in poetic and rhetorical prose: how to select and combine incidents, use images and figures of speech, employ amplification, and modulate style to move and enthral an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of the most striking circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: One cause of sublimity is the choice of the most striking circumstances involved in whatever we are describing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the vivid, powerful features actually exhibited in the situation (Sappho example). The reader is attracted partly by the selection of incidents; pick strokes observed in reality and those most likely to affect the emotions. Avoid including merely decorative or irrelevant details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining incidents into one animate whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to combine the striking circumstances afterwards into one animate whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weld selected incidents together skillfully so they cohere as a living picture. The effect depends both on what is chosen and on the skill with which they are united ("skill which has welded them together").

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject non-essential, frivolous, or tiresome interpositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors 'fastidiously reject whatever is not essential to the subject' because such blemishes mar the general effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against anything frivolous, unbecoming, or tiresome that interrupts the edifice of sublimity; such intrusions give a 'patched and gaping appearance'. Keep the structure solid and uniform; omit details that dilute or distract from the central effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplification must be supported by sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplification (bringing on one impressive point after another in a continuous and ascending scale) is incomplete without the aid of sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amplification gives extension and requires prolixity/diffusiveness; remove the element of sublimity and amplification becomes lifeless and dull. Use sublimity as the 'soul' of amplification except where the aim is simple pity or depreciation of an opponent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sublimity from amplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity gives elevation to a subject, while amplification gives extension as well; the sublime can be often conveyed in a single thought, amplification requires prolixity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sublime moments for elevation and concentrated force; use amplification where extended emphasis and accumulation of topics are needed. Choose the mode (sudden/high-strung vs. diffusive/extended) appropriate to the effect desired (e.g., Demosthenes vs. Cicero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of great writers as a path to sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Emulous imitation of the great poets and prose-writers of the past (Homer, Plato, Demosthenes, etc.) is a means to attain sublime heights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and imagine how canonical authors would have expressed a thought; copy from fair forms as from statues—not plagiarism but learning by emulation. Use models as beacons to guide and elevate one’s work; consider how future ages or great predecessors would judge the writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper employment of images (imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Images (all thoughts presented so as to issue in speech) are crucial to the dignity, grandeur, and energy of style; poetry uses images to astound, oratory to give perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce an illusion of seeing what is spoken of so hearers/readers 'almost see' the image. In poetry images may exceed logical credence; in oratory images should be energetic and realistic, not fabulous impossibilities. Match the image-type to purpose (astound vs. clarify).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt intensity and shaping of images to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Images must be suited to theme: heroic themes admit bold images; extravagant or unshapen images should be softened or avoided in inappropriate contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aeschylus' bold, rugged images suit heroic subjects; Euripides sometimes softens extravagant images when borrowing. Avoid unshapen, rough-hewn images where refinement or plausibility is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures of speech judiciously and in disguise
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures, judiciously employed, lend sublimity, but figures risk arousing suspicion of artifice and dishonesty, especially before judges or powerful hearers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures are most effectual when their artifice is masked by sublimity and passion; let grandeur 'shed its light' so the audience perceives the figure as inspired rather than scheming. Do not let figures appear as manipulative sophistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of adjuration / apostrophe (oath) in the right place
rubrics_metrics.description: The figure of adjuration or apostrophe (swearing by ancestors, invoking the dead) can exalt and emotionally move an audience when employed at the proper place, manner, occasion, and motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ oath/adjuration to elevate examples into near-divinity (as Demosthenes did), but choose words carefully to avoid giving opponents a handle; e.g., suppress terms (like 'conquered') that would spoil an intended parallel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical question and self-interrogation
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of question and interrogation stir an audience and give energy, especially when the orator replies to himself as if meeting objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rapid alternation of question and answer to simulate the natural moment of passion and to make speech seem spontaneous; this blinds judgment and persuades by apparent immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of connecting particles (asyndeton) for rush and urgency
rubrics_metrics.description: The removal of connecting particles gives a quick rush and 'torrent rapture' to a passage, making speech seem hurried and agitated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use asyndeton (omitting conjunctions/stops) to convey haste and emotional overwhelm (e.g., 'they pushed, they fought, they slew, they fell'), but apply sparingly—overuse can become monotonous or wear thin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine different figures to increase force and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining two or three figures mutually contributes to vigour, cogency, and beauty; repetition, breaking up sentences, and varying movement prevent rhetorical stillness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fuse repetition, asyndeton, interrogation, apostrophe, etc., to imitate agitation and to 'deal blow upon blow' upon the audience's mind. Vary rhythm and form to avoid stillness; use contrast, repetition in different forms, and sudden attacks to sustain momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use syntax and diction to imitate emotion (e.g., opposites, forceful prepositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bold and forcible combinations of words (such as prepositions of opposite meaning) can 'torture' language to imitate the agony or anxiety of a scene, stamping diction with the peculiar terror of the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange syntax and select diction to mirror psychological states (constraint, terror, agitation). Avoid hedging or mitigators that dissipate the intended feeling (contrast Aratus' 'frail timber shields' vs. Homer's unbounded peril).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix imagery with practical argument to enthral
rubrics_metrics.description: An oratorical image mingled with the practical, argumentative parts of an oration does not merely convince but enthralls the hearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed striking images within proofs so the stronger emotional force absorbs lesser logical objections; imagery should complement, not replace, argument. Ensure the image arises from the occasion so it appears natural rather than laboured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match style to authorial condition and subject (action vs narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style ought to suit the stage of genius and subject: works founded on action and struggle (Iliad) use different methods than narrative and delineation of character (Odyssey; age of genius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose action-driven, rapid, incident-filled diction when youthful/inspired power is available; prefer narrative, delineation, and comedy-of-manners when the author turns to character and quieter scope. Let the natural temperament and purpose determine pitch and strain.
